A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DMPEL and retain corresponding methods, experiments, and appendices. Text extraction and visual inspection support comparison of the equations, algorithms, tables, and figures despite substantial layout changes.

before.justification: v2 reports original LIBERO experiments, ablations, expert visualizations, and a 30-task continual-learning evaluation in Section 5 and Appendix B.

after.justification: v3 retains original LIBERO results and adds experiments including rank controls, separate-policy comparisons, larger-router evaluation, and Robomimic adaptation.

M1.justification: The policy architecture, dynamic expert mixture, orthogonal initialization, expert freezing, and coefficient-replay objective are retained. Pruning already appears in v2 Figure 6b and Appendix B.1; v3 provides its threshold and router-dimension handling without establishing a change to the underlying method.

E1.justification: Appendix B.5 adds three Robomimic tasks—Lift, Can, and Square—with novel backgrounds and objects but the same observation and action spaces. This modestly extends coverage beyond LIBERO. The four LIBERO suites, LIBERO-90 pretraining, and 30-task concatenation were already present.

E2.justification: Table 6 adds separate ViT-T policies with 1.9M and 17.7M parameters as comparators. Figure 7 adds ER and EWC to the embedding comparison, which previously included only DMPEL and SeqFT (LoRA). The main Figure 3 comparator set is retained.

E3.justification: v3 adds Final SR to the main evaluation and substantially expands controlled settings: tripled baseline ranks, different training/evaluation top-k combinations, separate-policy size controls, and a router with twice the depth and width. These supplement the existing experiments; the stated default training budget, optimizer, and evaluation frequency remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New analyses test rank/capacity explanations, routing mismatch, larger-router behavior, expert similarity, context–activation correlation, and action-space coverage. Activation case studies and embedding comparisons are expanded. Existing task-order, demonstration-count, pruning, and 30-task analyses are retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Appendix B.3 newly reports Pearson correlation estimation between context-embedding and expert-activation similarities, approximately 0.46. Repeated-run and uncertainty practices remain unchanged: both versions report means and standard deviations over seeds 100, 200, and 300.

E6.justification: Figure 3 adds Final SR and revises existing reported DMPEL values, including Long FWT from 53 to 55 and Object NBT from 7 to 4 under unchanged stated settings. Tables 4–8 add substantial results; for example, Robomimic AUC is 0.54 for DMPEL and TAIL versus 0.48 for IsCiL. The PDFs do not establish whether revised existing values reflect corrections or reruns.

T1.justification: Section 3.2 explicitly adds the Final SR definition, while Appendix C.1 develops a quantitative scaling argument for synthesis overhead relative to a backbone layer, including a 6.3% example. The earlier MDP, losses, mixture equations, and transfer metrics are otherwise retained with notation changes; no new theorem or proof appears.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: dynamically combining progressive low-rank experts for forward transfer and using coefficient replay to reduce forgetting efficiently without test-time task identifiers. Additional experiments support these claims without materially redefining them.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive interpretations of capacity controls, expert similarities, context-dependent activation, and router scaling. Appendix C expands the earlier brief limitations into discussions of computational/storage scaling and concrete sim2real obstacles. Section 5.2 also qualifies top-3 performance as comparable to using all experts, rather than simply better.

D1.justification: v3 documents the pruning threshold of 0.01, router-output management, and configurations for additional controls. Conversely, it removes v2's reproducibility statement and direct DMPEL code link. This changes reproducibility information, but does not establish that the repository itself became unavailable.

R1.justification: v3 adds citations including Ge et al. (2025) on continual multimodal LoRA experts, Mandlekar et al. (2022), Zhu et al. (2020), and action-control work by Zhao et al. (2023) and Chi et al. (2025). The overall positioning relative to PEFT, lifelong learning, and model fusion remains stable.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and much existing prose remain intact. v3 clarifies method and analysis passages, moves training pseudocode into the main text, reorganizes Appendix B, and separates the conclusion from limitations. It also removes the reproducibility and LLM-writing disclosures and updates publication and affiliation text.

P2.justification: Figure 3 gains a fourth metric column, Figure 7 expands to four methods, and activation visualizations gain tasks and modules. v3 adds five tables and several analytical plots, relocates existing material, and adopts a different journal layout. Retained learning curves are relocated without result changes. Figure 13 incorrectly captions its correlation plot as action trajectories.

improvement.justification: Tables 4–6 strengthen the comparisons through rank/capacity and routing controls, while Table 8 adds limited cross-domain evidence beyond v2's LIBERO study. Expanded limitations better distinguish demonstrated results from prospective scaling and real-robot use. These improve evidential support and clarity, although removing direct code-access information and miscaptioning Figure 13 partly offset the gains.
